claim: Septin proteins bind guanine nucleotides and form rod-shaped hetero-oligomers.
source: Septin proteins bind guanine nucleotides and form rod-shaped hetero-oligomers.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing fundamental properties of septin proteins.

claim: A stepwise assembly pathway produces the two species of budding yeast septin hetero-octamers: Cdc11/Shs1–Cdc12–Cdc3–Cdc10–Cdc10–Cdc3–Cdc12–Cdc11/Shs1.
source: Using a new in vivo assay, we find that a stepwise assembly pathway produces the two species of budding yeast septin hetero-octamers: Cdc11/Shs1–Cdc12–Cdc3–Cdc10–Cdc10–Cdc3–Cdc12–Cdc11/Shs1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the CSD-BiFC experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Rapid GTP hydrolysis by monomeric Cdc10 drives assembly of the core Cdc10 homodimer.
source: Rapid GTP hydrolysis by monomeric Cdc10 drives assembly of the core Cdc10 homodimer.
evidence: This is supported by CSD-BiFC data showing Cdc10-Cdc10 interaction precedes Cdc10-Cdc3 interaction, and by the D182N mutation experiments.

claim: The extended Cdc3 N terminus autoinhibits Cdc3 association with Cdc10 homodimers until prior Cdc3–Cdc12 interaction.
source: The extended Cdc3 N terminus autoinhibits Cdc3 association with Cdc10 homodimers until prior Cdc3–Cdc12 interaction.
evidence: This is supported by CSD-BiFC experiments showing that deletion of the Cdc3 NTE reverses the order of Cdc3 interactions, and by the ability of the NTE to shield NBP mutations.

claim: Slow hydrolysis by monomeric Cdc12 and specific affinity of Cdc11 for transient Cdc12•GTP drive assembly of distinct trimers, Cdc11–Cdc12–Cdc3 or Shs1–Cdc12–Cdc3.
source: Slow hydrolysis by monomeric Cdc12 and specific affinity of Cdc11 for transient Cdc12•GTP drive assembly of distinct trimers, Cdc11–Cdc12–Cdc3 or Shs1–Cdc12–Cdc3.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with Cdc12ΔCTE, Cdc12(T75A), and Cdc12(D104A) mutations showing altered Cdc11/Shs1 incorporation ratios.

claim: Decreasing the cytosolic GTP:GDP ratio increases the incorporation of Shs1 vs Cdc11.
source: Decreasing the cytosolic GTP:GDP ratio increases the incorporation of Shs1 vs Cdc11, which alters the curvature of filamentous septin rings.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with MPA treatment, carbon starvation, and respiratory growth conditions showing increased Shs1 and decreased Cdc11 incorporation.

claim: Altering the Shs1:Cdc11 ratio alters the curvature of filamentous septin rings.
source: Decreasing the cytosolic GTP:GDP ratio increases the incorporation of Shs1 vs Cdc11, which alters the curvature of filamentous septin rings.
evidence: This is supported by measurements of split ring diameter under different conditions that alter the Shs1:Cdc11 ratio.

claim: The septin family of cytoskeletal proteins is highly conserved between humans, yeast, and other non-plant eukaryotes, both in structure and function.
source: The septin family of cytoskeletal proteins is highly conserved between humans, yeast, and other non-plant eukaryotes, both in structure and function (Oh and Bi, 2011; Mostowy and Cossart, 2012; Dolat et al., 2014; Fung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Septins have been implicated in ciliogenesis, cytokinesis, microtubule dynamics, and neuronal development.
source: Septins have been implicated in a variety of processes, including ciliogenesis, cytokinesis, microtubule dynamics, and neuronal development (Oh and Bi, 2011; Mostowy and Cossart, 2012; Dolat et al., 2014; Fung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Septin dysfunction is linked to cancer, male infertility, and hereditary neuralgic amyotrophy.
source: Consequently, septin dysfunction is linked to a wide variety of human diseases, including cancer, male infertility, and hereditary neuralgic amyotrophy (Oh and Bi, 2011; Mostowy and Cossart, 2012; Dolat et al., 2014; Fung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There are 13 septin genes in humans, many of which have multiple distinct splice variants.
source: The diversity of functions correlates with the variety of septin monomers (13 in humans, many of which have multiple distinct splice variants) that create many different oligomer species.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about human septin genes.

claim: The majority of human septins are constitutively expressed across all cell types.
source: The majority of human septins are constitutively expressed across all cell types (Mostowy and Cossart, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Septins were first identified in Saccharomyces cerevisiae as temperature-sensitive mutants in which cytokinesis and bud morphogenesis are perturbed at the restrictive temperature.
source: Septins were first identified in Saccharomyces cerevisiae as temperature-sensitive mutants in which cytokinesis and bud morphogenesis are perturbed at the restrictive temperature (Hartwell, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: Five septin proteins are expressed in proliferating yeast cells: Cdc3, Cdc10, Cdc11, Cdc12, and Shs1.
source: Consistent with functions in cell division and morphogenesis, the five septin proteins expressed in proliferating yeast cells – Cdc3, Cdc10, Cdc11, Cdc12, and Shs1 – co-localize in filamentous, ring-like structures at the mother-bud neck (Oh and Bi, 2011; Glomb and Gronemeyer, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast septins, supported by citations.

claim: Yeast septin proteins co-localize in filamentous, ring-like structures at the mother-bud neck.
source: Consistent with functions in cell division and morphogenesis, the five septin proteins expressed in proliferating yeast cells – Cdc3, Cdc10, Cdc11, Cdc12, and Shs1 – co-localize in filamentous, ring-like structures at the mother-bud neck (Oh and Bi, 2011; Glomb and Gronemeyer, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast septin localization, supported by citations.

claim: Yeast septin rings act as plasma membrane diffusion barriers and scaffolds for the recruitment of other factors.
source: Yeast septin rings act as plasma membrane diffusion barriers and scaffolds for the recruitment of other factors (Oh and Bi, 2011; Glomb and Gronemeyer, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The five yeast septin proteins co-assemble into two different species of linear, palindromic hetero-octamers that act as the basic building blocks of septin filaments.
source: The five yeast septin proteins co-assemble into two different species of linear, palindromic hetero-octamers that act as the basic building blocks of septin filaments (i.e. protofilaments, [Oh and Bi, 2011; Glomb and Gronemeyer, 2016]) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The paralogs Shs1 and Cdc11 compete for occupancy of the terminal subunit positions in yeast septin hetero-octamers.
source: The paralogs Shs1 and Cdc11 compete for occupancy of the terminal subunit positions (McMurray et al., 2011; Finnigan et al., 2015; Garcia et al., 2011; Iwase et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The two protofilament species (Cdc11-capped and Shs1-capped) make distinct but poorly understood structural and functional contributions within filamentous septin rings.
source: These two protofilament species make distinct but poorly understood structural and functional contributions within filamentous septin rings (McMurray et al., 2011; Finnigan et al., 2015; Garcia et al., 2011; Iwase et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MPA treatment significantly depleted BiFC signals at septin rings and in the cytosol for most septin-septin interactions.
source: Consistent with a requirement for nucleotide binding for both G and NC interfaces, MPA treatment significantly depleted BiFC signals, both at septin rings and in the cytosol, generated from interactions via either interface (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: BiFC signal from Shs1–Cdc12 interaction was equivalent in untreated and MPA-treated cells.
source: The notable exception was BiFC signal from Shs1–Cdc12, a G dimer, which was equivalent in untreated and treated cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: MPA treatment at 100 µg/ml slows but does not halt cell division, and septin ring morphology, bud growth, mitosis progression, and cytokinesis completion are all unperturbed.
source: At this concentration MPA slows, but does not halt, cell division, and septin ring morphology, the growth of buds, the progression of mitosis, and completion of cytokinesis are all unperturbed (Sagot et al., 2005; Escobar-Henriques et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MPA has negligible effects on the septin-recruiting GTPase Cdc42.
source: Thus, MPA has negligible effects on the septin-recruiting GTPase Cdc42, which in any case is thought to act on septins only following assembly (Sadian et al., 2013; Okada et al., 2013), and all available evidence suggests that, following translation (the efficiency of which is decreased by MPA (Escobar-Henriques et al., 2001)), the only proteins that must bind guanine nucleotides in order to promote septin protofilament assembly are the septins themselves.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited literature and the experimental conditions.

claim: Cdc12-VC first dimerizes with Cdc11-CN at the G interface before subsequent NC interaction with Cdc3-VN.
source: Interrogation of Cdc12–Cdc11 (G interface) and Cdc12–Cdc3 (NC interface) revealed that Cdc12-VC first dimerized with Cdc11-CN at the G interface before subsequent NC interaction with Cdc3-VN, as evidenced by depletion of the yellow signal and maintenance of the blue signal (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CSD-BiFC data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cdc3-VC first interacts with Cdc12-VN (NC interface) before interacting with Cdc10-CN (G interface).
source: By contrast, our CSD-BiFC data suggest that Cdc3-VC first interacts with Cdc12-VN (NC interface) before interacting with Cdc10-CN (G interface) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CSD-BiFC data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cdc3 oligomerizes robustly with Cdc12 in yeast cells carrying Cdc10 mutations inhibiting G dimerization.
source: This departure from NC priming was not unexpected, as Cdc3 oligomerizes robustly with Cdc12 both in yeast cells carrying Cdc10 mutations inhibiting G dimerization (Nagaraj et al., 2008) and during heterologous co-expression without Cdc10 in E. coli (Versele et al., 2004; Farkasovsky et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cdc3 oligomerizes with Cdc12 during heterologous co-expression without Cdc10 in E. coli.
source: This departure from NC priming was not unexpected, as Cdc3 oligomerizes robustly with Cdc12 both in yeast cells carrying Cdc10 mutations inhibiting G dimerization (Nagaraj et al., 2008) and during heterologous co-expression without Cdc10 in E. coli (Versele et al., 2004; Farkasovsky et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cdc3 lacks the highly conserved Thr residue important for GTP hydrolysis in human septins.
source: Moreover, Cdc3 lacks the highly conserved Thr residue important for GTP hydrolysis in human septins (Sirajuddin et al., 2009) and purified Cdc3 does not hydrolyze GTP in vitro (Versele and Thorner, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Purified Cdc3 does not hydrolyze GTP in vitro.
source: Moreover, Cdc3 lacks the highly conserved Thr residue important for GTP hydrolysis in human septins (Sirajuddin et al., 2009) and purified Cdc3 does not hydrolyze GTP in vitro (Versele and Thorner, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Cdc10-VC interacts first with Cdc10-CN (NC interface) before interacting with Cdc3-VN (G interface).
source: To our surprise, no other septin-septin interaction conformed to the NC priming model. Our data suggested that Cdc10-VC interacts first with Cdc10-CN (NC interface) before interacting with Cdc3-VN (G interface), and that Cdc12-VC interacts first with Cdc3-VN (NC interface) before interacting with Shs1-CN (G interface) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CSD-BiFC data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cdc12-VC interacts first with Cdc3-VN (NC interface) before interacting with Shs1-CN (G interface).
source: To our surprise, no other septin-septin interaction conformed to the NC priming model. Our data suggested that Cdc10-VC interacts first with Cdc10-CN (NC interface) before interacting with Cdc3-VN (G interface), and that Cdc12-VC interacts first with Cdc3-VN (NC interface) before interacting with Shs1-CN (G interface) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CSD-BiFC data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cdc12 NC oligomerization with Cdc3 requires G interaction when the G partner is Cdc11, but not when the G partner is Shs1.
source: These results indicate that Cdc10 NC homodimerization does not require prior G oligomerization with Cdc3 and, intriguingly, that Cdc12 NC oligomerization with Cdc3 requires G interaction when the G partner is Cdc11, but not when the G partner is Shs1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the CSD-BiFC data comparing Cdc12 interactions with Cdc11 vs Shs1.

claim: Monomeric Cdc10 and Cdc12 (but not Cdc11 or Cdc3) are capable of GTP hydrolysis in vitro.
source: In support of this idea, monomeric Cdc10 and Cdc12 (but not Cdc11 or Cdc3) are capable of GTP hydrolysis in vitro (Versele and Thorner, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The cdc10(D182N) allele prevents binding of guanine nucleotides.
source: To this end, we used a substitution in the Cdc10 NBP, D182N, that prevents binding of guanine nucleotides (Weems et al., 2014; Kuo et al., 2012), and queried the order of Cdc10(D182N)-VC interaction with Cdc3-VN and/or Cdc10-CN.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Yellow fluorescence due to Cdc10(D182N)-VC–Cdc3-VN interaction was depleted by co-expression of Cdc10-CN, and blue fluorescence from Cdc10-CN–Cdc10-VC interaction was depleted by co-expression of Cdc3-VN.
source: As predicted, yellow fluorescence due to Cdc10(D182N)-VC–Cdc3-VN interaction was depleted by co-expression of Cdc10-CN, and blue fluorescence from Cdc10-CN–Cdc10-VC interaction was depleted by co-expression of Cdc3-VN (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CSD-BiFC data shown in Figure 3.

claim: When expressed as the sole source of Cdc10, the cdc10(D182N) allele provides largely normal function at low temperatures.
source: When expressed as the sole source of Cdc10, the cdc10(D182N) allele provides largely normal function at low temperatures (Hartwell, 1971; Weems et al., 2014; Johnson et al., 2015), demonstrating that nucleotide binding and hydrolysis by Cdc10 are not absolutely required for septin hetero-octamer or filament assembly.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The rate of GTP hydrolysis by purified Cdc12 is approximately half that of Cdc10.
source: The rate of GTP hydrolysis by purified Cdc12 is approximately half that of Cdc10 (Versele and Thorner, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Truncation of the Cdc12 CTE accelerates GTP hydrolysis in vitro.
source: Truncation of the Cdc12 CTE accelerates GTP hydrolysis in vitro (Versele and Thorner, 2004), providing a genetic approach to test our model, according to the following logic.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In cells with a Cdc12ΔCTE plasmid, Shs1 incorporation was significantly increased compared to cells with a WT Cdc12 plasmid, and Cdc11 was correspondingly depleted.
source: In agreement with our prediction, in cells with a Cdc12∆CTE plasmid, Shs1 incorporation was significantly increased compared to cells with a WT Cdc12 plasmid, and Cdc11 was correspondingly depleted (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C (though the figure reference appears to be 4B based on the figure labels).

claim: Cdc12ΔCTE-VC–Cdc11-VN signal was reduced compared to Cdc12-VC–Cdc11-VN controls, and Cdc12ΔCTE-VC–Shs1-VN was elevated compared to Cdc12-VC–Shs1-VN.
source: To corroborate these results using an alternate approach, we assayed Cdc12–Shs1/Cdc11 interactions via BiFC. Cdc12ΔCTE-VC–Cdc11-VN signal was reduced compared to Cdc12-VC–Cdc11-VN controls, and Cdc12ΔCTE-VC–Shs1-VN was elevated compared to Cdc12-VC–Shs1-VN (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the BiFC data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In cells expressing cdc12(T75A), Cdc11 incorporation into neck filaments was significantly reduced, and Shs1 was correspondingly increased.
source: Consistent with a predicted depletion of Cdc12•GTP, in cells expressing cdc12(T75A) Cdc11 incorporation into neck filaments was significantly reduced, and Shs1 was correspondingly increased (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cdc11 and Shs1 were both depleted from neck filaments in cells expressing Cdc12(G268R).
source: By contrast, Cdc11 and Shs1 were both depleted from neck filaments in cells expressing Cdc12(G268R) (Figure 4E), a mutant with a substitution in a key component of the G interface (the Sep4 motif) that lies outside the NBP and does not change conformation upon GTP hydrolysis (Sirajuddin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In cdc12(G268R) cells, the relative ratio between Cdc11 and Shs1 (Cdc11:Shs1 ≅ 1.6:1) was preserved.
source: Interestingly, although levels of both Cdc11 and Shs1 in septin rings were reduced in cdc12(G268R) cells, the relative ratio between the two proteins (Cdc11:Shs1 ≅ 1.6:1) was preserved.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cdc11 incorporation into septin rings decreased in cdc12(D104A) cells, and Shs1 incorporation increased.
source: In support of our model, Cdc11 incorporation into septin rings decreased in cdc12(D104A) cells, and Shs1 incorporation increased (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: High-level overexpression of Cdc11 or Shs1 is toxic.
source: High-level overexpression of Cdc11 or Shs1 is toxic (Iwase et al., 2007; Sopko et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Overexpression of Cdc11-GFP or Shs1-GFP from low-copy plasmids increased cytosolic fluorescence significantly but there was no discernable difference in the GFP signal in septin rings.
source: Indeed, cytosolic fluorescence increased significantly (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Crucially, however, there was no discernable difference in the GFP signal in septin rings (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Cdc3 NTE is predicted to be almost entirely disordered.
source: The Cdc3 NTE is predicted to be almost entirely disordered (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational prediction shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Sequence alignments with other fungal species revealed considerable drift in the NTEs of otherwise closely related Cdc3 homologs, yet the disordered character was uniformly maintained.
source: Sequence alignments with other fungal species revealed considerable drift in the NTEs of otherwise closely related Cdc3 homologs, yet the disordered character was uniformly maintained (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: For Cdc10, Cdc11, and Cdc12, single NBP mutations are sufficient to slow the maturation of the mutant septin to a conformation capable of G dimerization with other septins.
source: To look for evidence that the NTE transiently occupies the Cdc3 G interface prior to Cdc3 interaction with other septins, we considered that for Cdc10, Cdc11, and Cdc12, single NBP mutations are sufficient to slow the maturation of the mutant septin to a conformation capable of G dimerization with other septins (Nagaraj et al., 2008; Johnson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: For Cdc3, only a triple NBP mutation (G129V K132E T133N) sufficed to render the mutant less able to 'compete' with WT Cdc3 for incorporation into higher-order septin assemblies.
source: Yet for Cdc3 only a triple NBP mutation (G129V K132E T133N) sufficed to render the mutant less able to 'compete' with WT Cdc3 for incorporation into higher-order septin assemblies (Nagaraj et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Cdc3(D289N)-GFP was incorporated efficiently into septin rings, equivalent to the behavior of WT Cdc3-GFP tested in the same way.
source: Unlike Cdc10(D182N)-GFP, which is sequestered in the cytosol (Johnson et al., 2015), Cdc3(D289N)-GFP was incorporated efficiently into septin rings, equivalent to the behavior of WT Cdc3-GFP tested in the same way (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cdc3(∆1–100 D289N)-GFP was unable to localize to the septin ring in WT cells.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the NTE was required for efficient higher-order incorporation by Cdc3(D289N) in the presence of WT Cdc3, as Cdc3(∆1–100 D289N)-GFP was unable to localize to the septin ring in WT cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cdc3(∆1–56 D289N)-GFP localized robustly to septin rings.
source: Even a partially truncated NTE was able to shield Cdc3(D289N) from cytosolic sequestration, as Cdc3(∆1–56 D289N)-GFP localized robustly to septin rings (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cdc3(∆1–100)-GFP incorporated normally into septin rings.
source: Importantly, however, NTE truncation did not itself compromise higher order assembly by Cdc3, because Cdc3(∆1–100)-GFP incorporated normally into septin rings (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When expressed as the sole source of Cdc3, the cdc3(Δ1–100 D289N) allele provided normal septin function under the same conditions in which the co-expression experiments were performed.
source: Finally, the Cdc3(Δ1–100 D289N) mutant protein was not simply incapable of higher order assembly, because when expressed as the sole source of Cdc3 this allele provided normal septin function under the same conditions in which the co-expression experiments were performed (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: cdc3(Δ1–100 D289N) cells were unable to proliferate at 30°C.
source: Like cdc10(D182N) cells, but unlike cells in which either the Cdc3 NBP or the NTE was intact, cdc3(Δ1–100 D289N) cells were unable to proliferate at 30°C (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Expression of Cdc10-CN depleted the signal arising from Cdc3(Δ1–100)-VC–Cdc12-VN interaction, whereas Cdc3(Δ1–100)-VC–Cdc10-CN signal was unaffected by expression of Cdc12-VN.
source: As predicted, expression of Cdc10-CN depleted the signal arising from Cdc3(Δ1–100)-VC–Cdc12-VN interaction, whereas Cdc3(Δ1–100)-VC–Cdc10-CN signal was unaffected by expression of Cdc12-VN (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the CSD-BiFC data shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: The cytosolic ratio of GTP to GDP is subject to large variations under different cellular conditions, both in budding yeast and human cells.
source: While the cytosolic ratio of GTP to GDP is often assumed to be fixed at a high value, in fact this ratio is subject to large variations under different cellular conditions, both in budding yeast (Saint-Marc et al., 2009; Rudoni et al., 2001) and human cells (Meshkini, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MPA treatment significantly reduces the ratio of GTP:GDP in the residual nucleotide pool to nearly 1, compared to >3:1 in untreated, fermentatively growing cultures.
source: MPA treatment not only depletes guanine nucleotides, it also significantly reduces the ratio of GTP:GDP in the residual nucleotide pool to nearly 1, compared to >3:1 in untreated, fermentatively growing cultures (Saint-Marc et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: MPA treatment reduced Cdc11-GFP signal in septin rings and increased Shs1-GFP signal.
source: Consistent with our prediction, MPA treatment reduced Cdc11-GFP signal in septin rings and increased Shs1-GFP signal (Figure 6A), mirroring with WT cells the results of mutating Cdc12 (Figure 4B,D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Reducing the concentration of fermentable carbon (dextrose) downregulates IMPDH expression and reduces the GTP:GDP ratio.
source: Reducing the concentration of fermentable carbon (dextrose) downregulates IMPDH expression (Bradley et al., 2009) and reduces the GTP:GDP ratio (Rudoni et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: IMPDH expression decreases when dextrose is replaced with glycerol.
source: IMPDH expression also decreases when dextrose is replaced with glycerol (Roberts and Hudson, 2006), a non-fermentable carbon source.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Both 0.1% dextrose and 3% glycerol reduced Cdc11-GFP and increased Shs1-GFP incorporation into septin rings.
source: Both 0.1% dextrose and 3% glycerol reduced Cdc11-GFP and increased Shs1-GFP incorporation into septin rings (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6B and 6C (the text references 6C,D but likely means 6B,C based on figure labels).

claim: In neither 0.1% dextrose nor 3% glycerol conditions does the level of Shs1 or Cdc11 (as indicated by mRNA levels) change significantly.
source: Importantly, in neither condition does the level of Shs1 or Cdc11 (as indicated by mRNA levels) change significantly (Roberts and Hudson, 2006; Tai et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: When shs1∆ mutants of the BY4741 strain background are cultured at moderate temperatures in 2% dextrose, bud morphology and septin ring assembly are largely normal.
source: When shs1∆ mutants of the BY4741 strain background are cultured at moderate temperatures in 2% dextrose, bud morphology and septin ring assembly (as observed by light microscopy) are largely normal (Finnigan et al., 2015) (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and the data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Elongated cells were frequent (~20%) in shs1∆ mutants cultured in low dextrose or glycerol.
source: In contrast, elongated cells were frequent (~20%) in shs1∆ mutants cultured in low dextrose or glycerol.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Misshapen septin rings were far more prevalent in shs1∆ cells cultured in glycerol or low dextrose.
source: Moreover, as visualized with fluorescently tagged Cdc3 encoded by a plasmid, misshapen septin rings were far more prevalent in shs1∆ cells cultured in glycerol or low dextrose (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Purified, recombinant hetero-octamers containing Cdc11 at both ends form straight filaments with little curvature in the absence of membranes.
source: In the absence of membranes, purified, recombinant hetero-octamers containing Cdc11 at both ends form straight filaments with little curvature (Garcia et al., 2011; Sirajuddin et al., 2007; Frazier et al., 1998; Sadian et al., 2013; Bertin et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Titrating in Shs1-capped hetero-octamers promotes the assembly of curved filaments and, at high Shs1:Cdc11 ratios, rings of diameter ~0.3 µm.
source: Titrating in Shs1-capped hetero-octamers promotes the assembly of curved filaments and, at high Shs1:Cdc11 ratios, rings of diameter ~0.3 µm (Garcia et al., 2011), considerably smaller than the ~1 µm diameter of septin rings in WT yeast cells (Okada et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cdc11-capped hetero-octamers associate preferentially with membrane-coated beads of diameter ~1 µm, and have little affinity for 0.3 µm beads.
source: Cdc11-capped hetero-octamers associate preferentially with membrane-coated beads of diameter ~1 µm, and have little affinity for 0.3 µm beads (Bridges et al., 2016); Shs1-capped octamers have not been tested in this way.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In shs1∆ cdc11∆ cells, septin filaments are no longer restricted to the most highly curved regions of the bud necks.
source: Indeed, in shs1∆ cdc11∆ cells septin filaments are no longer restricted to the most highly curved regions of the bud necks (McMurray et al., 2011; Iwase et al., 2007), and in cells of the filamentous fungus Ashbya gosyppii, the presence of WT Shs1 similarly appears to direct septin hetero-octamer recruitment to membrane regions with distinct curvatures (Meseroll et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The diameters of the yeast septin rings at the time of bud emergence and the diameter of the bud neck itself are functions of the activity of the small GTPase Cdc42.
source: Previous studies clearly established that the diameters of the yeast septin rings at the time of bud emergence (Okada et al., 2013) and the diameter of the bud neck itself (Gladfelter et al., 2005) are functions of the activity of the small GTPase Cdc42, and do not reflect intrinsic properties of the septin filaments themselves (although Shs1/Cdc11 composition might dictate the range of tolerable diameters).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Upon the onset of cytokinesis, the septin 'collar' at the bud neck splits into two rings flanking the hourglass-shaped bud neck.
source: On the other hand, upon the onset of cytokinesis, the septin 'collar' at the bud neck splits into two rings flanking the hourglass-shaped bud neck (Lippincott and Li, 1998; Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Split septin ring diameter decreased in every situation in which the Shs1:Cdc11 ratio increased.
source: Split septin ring diameter decreased in every situation in which the Shs1:Cdc11 ratio increased (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6E (the text references 6G but likely means 6E based on figure labels).

claim: Split septin rings were smaller in cdc12(D104A) cells cultured in 2% dextrose.
source: However, split septin rings were also smaller in cdc12(D104A) cells cultured in 2% dextrose (Figure 6E), arguing against these explanations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: By EM tomography, septin filaments are grossly disorganized at the necks of shs1∆ cells grown in 2% dextrose, yet buds are round.
source: By EM tomography, septin filaments are grossly disorganized at the necks of shs1∆ cells grown in 2% dextrose, yet buds are round (Garcia et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The very first GTP hydrolysis event catalyzed by a nascent tubulin polypeptide takes place concomitantly with α-β heterodimerization and triggers heterodimer release from a complex with tubulin folding cofactors.
source: Importantly, however, the very first GTP hydrolysis event catalyzed by a nascent tubulin polypeptide takes place concomitantly with α-β heterodimerization and triggers heterodimer release from a complex with tubulin folding cofactors (Tian et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In vitro filament assembly and disassembly by septin hetero-octamers is controlled by the ionic strength of the buffer with no requirement for exogenous GTP.
source: Similarly, in vitro filament assembly and disassembly by septin hetero-octamers is controlled by the ionic strength of the buffer with no requirement for exogenous GTP (Frazier et al., 1998; Bertin et al., 2008; Booth et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cdc11 possesses in place of Lys an unusual P-loop Arg residue whose longer sidechain is predicted to occupy the space normally filled by the γ phosphate of GTP, making GTP binding unlikely.
source: Cdc11 possesses in place of Lys an unusual P-loop Arg residue whose longer sidechain is predicted to occupy the space normally filled by the γ phosphate of GTP, making GTP binding unlikely (Brausemann et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature and structural inference.

claim: At least 7 of the 13 human septin genes are transcribed in all tissues.
source: At least 7 of the 13 septin genes are transcribed in all tissues, with specific tissues expressing considerably more (Mostowy and Cossart, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: 12 of the 13 human septin genes are expressed in the central nervous system.
source: For instance, 12 of the 13 septin genes are expressed in the central nervous system (Mostowy and Cossart, 2012), and hippocampal neurons alone produce all 10 septins thus far queried by immunoblot (Tsang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Hippocampal neurons produce all 10 septins thus far queried by immunoblot.
source: For instance, 12 of the 13 septin genes are expressed in the central nervous system (Mostowy and Cossart, 2012), and hippocampal neurons alone produce all 10 septins thus far queried by immunoblot (Tsang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Specific septins are excluded from hetero-oligomers containing other septins with which the excluded proteins are clearly able to interact in other contexts.
source: However, not all septins produced in a given cell are incorporated into protofilaments: specific septins are excluded from hetero-oligomers containing other septins with which the excluded proteins are clearly able to interact in other contexts (Abbey et al., 2016; Sellin et al., 2014; Mizutani et al., 2013; Shinoda et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Five human septin genes (SEPT2, SEPT3, SEPT4, SEPT9, and SEPT10) have NTEs of at least ~43 amino acids.
source: Indeed, five human septin genes (SEPT2, SEPT3, SEPT4, SEPT9, and SEPT10) have NTEs of at least ~43 amino acids, similar to the region functional for G-occlusion in Cdc3.
evidence: This is a statement based on sequence analysis of human septin genes.

claim: For SEPT2, SEPT4, SEPT9, and SEPT10, splice variants halve the NTE or eliminate it altogether.
source: Moreover, for SEPT2, SEPT4, SEPT9, and SEPT10, splice variants halve the NTE or eliminate it altogether, hypothetically allowing alternative splicing to control whether G-occluding or non-G-occluding variants are expressed.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge of human septin splice variants.

claim: A SEPT7(S63A) mutation that doubles the rate of GTP hydrolysis in vitro shifts in vivo the specific SEPT9 splice variants with which it interacts.
source: Indeed, Abbey et al., 2016 found that a SEPT7(S63A) mutation that doubles the rate of GTP hydrolysis in vitro shifts in vivo the specific SEPT9 splice variants with which it interacts (via the G interface).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: An increase in the GTP:GDP ratio accompanying IMP dehydrogenase induction during proliferation might drive assembly of distinct septin protofilaments in human cells.
source: An increase in the GTP:GDP ratio accompanying IMP dehydrogenase induction during proliferation (Collart et al., 1992; Zimmermann et al., 1998) might drive assembly of distinct septin protofilaments in human cells.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the yeast data and cited literature about IMPDH induction.

claim: Viability and colony growth rates were unaffected by the BiFC tags.
source: Viability and colony growth rates were unaffected by the tags (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and elongated cells, a sensitive indicator of septin dysfunction (McMurray, 2016), were very rare (≤2%) and similar to what is observed for non-BiFC fluorophore fusions (Finnigan et al., 2015; McMurray, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The BiFC events analyzed did not perturb the normal dynamics of septin rings during the progression of bud growth and cytokinesis.
source: Finally, the BiFC events we analyzed did not perturb the normal dynamics of septin rings during the progression of bud growth and cytokinesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The isolated C-terminal extensions (CTEs) of Cdc3 and Cdc12 have weak affinity for each other.
source: Notably, although the isolated C-terminal extensions (CTEs) of Cdc3 and Cdc12 have weak affinity for each other (Versele et al., 2004), the fact that depleting nucleotides reduces Cdc3–Cdc12 BiFC argues that C-terminal BiFC tags must primarily report on authentic NC-interface-mediated interactions that are influenced allosterically by nucleotides in the NBPs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The Cdc12 CTE alone cannot incorporate into septin filaments.
source: Indeed, the Cdc12 CTE alone cannot incorporate into septin filaments (Versele et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The Cdc12∆CTE mutant is lethal as the sole source of Cdc12.
source: The Cdc12∆CTE mutant is lethal as the sole source of Cdc12 (Versele et al., 2004) and is dominantly lethal when highly overexpressed in WT cells (Johnson et al., 2015; Versele et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Cdc12∆CTE mutant is dominantly lethal when highly overexpressed in WT cells.
source: The Cdc12∆CTE mutant is lethal as the sole source of Cdc12 (Versele et al., 2004) and is dominantly lethal when highly overexpressed in WT cells (Johnson et al., 2015; Versele et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Septin C-terminal extensions (CTEs) are long and flexible.
source: Note that septin C-terminal extensions (CTEs) are long and flexible: GFP fused to the C terminus of the nematode septin UNC-61 rotates ~180˚ at a radius of ~10 nm from the ~4 nm-wide globular UNC-61 GTPase domain (John et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The CTE of UNC-61 is 100 residues, and those of Cdc3, Cdc11, Cdc12, and Shs1 are 110, 118, 94, and 233 residues, respectively.
source: Yeast septin CTEs, measured from the end of the α6 helix (Sirajuddin et al., 2007), are similarly long: that of UNC-61 is 100 residues, and those of Cdc3, Cdc11, Cdc12, and Shs1 are 110, 118, 94, and 233 residues, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement based on sequence analysis and structural knowledge.

claim: For the CTE-containing septins Cdc3, Cdc11, Cdc12, and Shs1, the Venus fragments will be located far from both the NC and G interfaces, and interactions across either interface should generate BiFC signals of similar strengths.
source: Thus, although the NC interface involves α6 residues, for the CTE-containing septins Cdc3, Cdc11, Cdc12, and Shs1, the Venus fragments will be located far from both the NC and G interfaces, and interactions across either interface should generate BiFC signals of similar strengths, as experimentally demonstrated here.
evidence: This claim is based on structural reasoning and is supported by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The BiFC signals measured reported primarily on interactions that occurred during previous cell cycles.
source: We note that, given the slow maturation of the reconstituted fluorophore following a BiFC event (~50 min [Kerppola, 2008]), compounded with long septin half-lives and septin 'recycling' through cell divisions (McMurray and Thorner, 2008), the BiFC signals we measured reported primarily on interactions that occurred during previous cell cycles.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited literature about BiFC maturation kinetics and septin dynamics.

claim: Yeast septins populate up to four distinct octameric protofilament species (counting the sporulation-specific subunits Spr3 and Spr28).
source: Counting the sporulation-specific subunits Spr3 and Spr28, yeast septins populate up to four distinct octameric protofilament species (Garcia et al., 2011; Bertin et al., 2008; Garcia et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: With 13 septin genes in humans, each possessing up to eight different splice variants, human cells could potentially assemble ≥4992 distinct protofilament species, considering only canonical palindromic octamers and hexamers.
source: Indeed, with 13 septin genes – each possessing up to eight different splice variants – human cells could potentially assemble ≥4992 distinct protofilament species, considering only canonical palindromic octamers and hexamers.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the known number of human septin genes and splice variants.

claim: Considerable evidence of stark functional variation between septin isoforms fits with observations of distinct septin structures and protofilaments in different cell types.
source: Considerable evidence of stark functional variation between septin isoforms fits with observations of distinct septin structures and protofilaments in different cell types and suggests cell-type-specific demands for different septin protofilaments (Mostowy and Cossart, 2012; Dolat et al., 2014; Saarikangas and Barral, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The SEPT9 NTE interacts with actin and microtubules, but the relevant sequences are restricted to the N-terminal half.
source: (The SEPT9 NTE interacts with actin (Smith et al., 2015) and microtubules (Bai et al., 2013), but the relevant sequences are restricted to the N-terminal half, while the C-terminal half fulfills the conditions described above.)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.
